SheetA-1
CourseMMAE 414 Aircraft Design I, fall 2025
DeliverablesCDR & Final Report
My partCDR: structures (primary) and propulsion (secondary). Final report: the Simulink flight model.
Methods & toolsRaymer's statistical sizing, W/S–P/W trade study, XFLR5, MATLAB/Simulink, SolidWorks

Project Dusty: a crop duster from sizing to flight simulation

Result in one lineA 16,767 lb turboprop crop duster sized with Raymer's methods, then flown through glide, climb, holding and landing in a 6DOF Simulink model. Climb rate 1,500 ft/min, altitude held within ±6 m in the holding pattern.

The brief was a crop duster that sprays a 400-acre square field on its own, but can carry a pilot to fly itself to a new site. It operates from Athol, Kansas, needs a 1,000 ft ground run and 1,500 ft total field length over a 50 ft obstacle, stays under 19,000 lb gross weight, and has a 600 nm ferry range. The engine had to be in production as of 2025 and able to burn sustainable aviation fuel.

We were given mission objectives and technical requirements similar to the AIAA Design/Build/Fly Competition. The project had two parts: the CDR, which yielded the preliminary configuration, and a final report which validates the result of various iterative processes and shows the aircraft flying.

Conceptual design review

We started from Raymer's statistical relations and comparisons with existing crop dusters, then ran a wing-loading and power-to-weight trade study. It produced two optimized aircraft, one for each candidate engine size. Both met takeoff, landing and speed requirements. We picked the heavier one using an engine selection matrix and a metric we called AAUM (how much wet load the aircraft can spray per day relative to its takeoff weight).

THE TWO OPTIMIZED DESIGNS FROM THE TRADE STUDY
Light, 1,050 hpHeavy, 1,295 hp (chosen)
Takeoff gross weight13,570 lb16,767 lb
Wing span / area57 ft / 358 ft²63 ft / 440 ft²
Hopper capacity540.5 gal675 gal
Maximum speed328.9 ft/s312.1 ft/s
AAUM0.39970.4201

Both designs: W/S about 38 lb/ft², P/W 0.0772, aspect ratio 9.

ENGINE SELECTION MATRIX (WEIGHTED SUM, HIGHER IS BETTER)
EnginePower (shp)Takeoff ground roll (ft)Score
P&W PT6A-65AG1,2959981.069
P&W PT6A-60AG1,0501,0060.988
P&W PT6A-140AG8671,0060.946
P&W PT6A-34AG7501,0060.943

Criteria were power, fuel consumption, engine weight and length, takeoff parameter, cost and ground roll. Only the 65AG met the 1,000 ft ground-run requirement.

The final CDR design: 16,767 lb takeoff weight (9,267 lb empty, 1,870 lb fuel, 5,630 lb payload on the spray mission), 63 ft span, 440 ft² wing, NACA 4415/4412 wing sections and NACA 0012 tails. Estimated flyaway cost is $17.8 million and operation and maintenance about $458k per year. On the propulsion side, the report sizes a 114 in five-blade propeller, with roughly 0.82 efficiency in cruise and a helical tip Mach number of 0.79.

My part: structures

I worked through weight, fuselage, pilot accommodation, landing gear and the V-n diagram.

  • Fuselage length: 37.84 ft from Raymer's statistical equation.
  • Pilot view: I computed an over-the-nose angle of 9.51° for a 93 kt, 3° approach. Because the aircraft is a taildragger, I raised it to 15° for landing visibility, with a 35° transparency angle and 40° over the side.
  • Landing gear: I chose a taildragger over a tricycle layout because it copes better with soft fields and is lighter and simpler. Gear position came from a moment balance about the CG: main gear 3.9 ft from the CG, tail wheel 22.1 ft, 26 ft between them.
  • Tires: main wheels 33.4 in diameter by 11.4 in wide (7,126 lb per wheel), tail wheel 10 in by 11 in.
  • V-n diagram: maximum load factor 3.8 and minimum −1.5, corner speed 261.4 ft/s, maximum speed 312 ft/s. The airframe life estimate came to 52,000 hours.

Flight simulation

For the final report we built a 6DOF aircraft model in Simulink. The aerodynamic derivatives (lift, drag, pitching moment, side force, yaw and roll moment against angle of attack, sideslip and control deflections) came from XFLR5 and sit in MATLAB look-up tables. Around the model we built the controllers: altitude hold with phugoid and pitch-rate damping on the elevator, roll angle hold with roll-rate damping on the ailerons and sideslip control with yaw damping on the rudder. Thrust is commanded separately for each flight phase.

We then flew four commanded trajectories.

The trajectories tracked the commanded paths closely, with small deviations in turns and transitions. A few decisions along the way mattered more than the final plots suggest:

  • A step altitude command made the elevator react too hard, giving unrealistic climb rates and velocity oscillations. Switching to a ramp fixed it.
  • During the landing descent the altitude controller pitched down and the aircraft sped up. We commanded reverse thrust (negative propeller pitch, possible on a turboprop) to hold the approach speed.
  • At lower speed the aircraft is more sensitive in roll and yaw, so the landing turns needed smaller bank angles and longer holds.
Sanity checkA 3°/s turn at 101 m/s needs a bank of atan(Vω/g) = 28.3°, which matches the 28° bank the roll controller held in the holding pattern.
What I'd revisit

Glide angle. Our report quoted a 1.53° glide angle next to an L/D of 26.4, but those two numbers do not go together. 1,524 m of altitude lost over 40,200 m is atan(1524/40200) = 2.17°, and 1.53° would imply an L/D near 37. The L/D of 26.4 is the number that follows from the plot, so I have corrected the angle here.

The glide L/D of 26.4 is higher than I would trust for an aircraft this size. We attributed it to XFLR5 leaving out parasitic drag from the fuselage and landing gear, as well as to its simplified handling of induced drag and separation. I would add that drag before relying on the glide numbers.

The glide also only settled when I raised the initial speed from the 82.7 m/s design cruise to 101 m/s, so the simulation ran at a different speed from the one the CDR was sized for. 101 m/s is also about 331 ft/s, above the 312 ft/s maximum speed in the CDR and V-n diagram. That mismatch should be resolved rather than worked around. Landing still showed some roll and yaw oscillation in the turns; it was damped compared to earlier attempts but not gone.

SheetM-1
CourseComputer-Aided Design and Manufacturing, spring 2025
ToolsSolidWorks, Mastercam
TaskTurn a provided CNC-milled arbor press body into a castable version and mold, check both by FEA and improve the design. Then produce drawings, assemblies and CAM programs.

Arbor press: from milled part to castable part

Result in one lineCast version brought from a safety factor of 0.78 to 1.03 by removing the spine, enlarging the arcs and widening the trunk. The milled version got 11% lighter but is still 11 MPa over yield.

I kept the milled, mold and cast versions as configurations of the same part, since they are different physical stages of one part. For the mold I added draft angles so the part releases from the mold instead of dragging along a full face. The order mattered: I suppressed the holes and slot, rolled the feature tree back to before the fillets so the draft would not fail on the blended surfaces, cut the part in half, applied draft to one side, checked it with the Draft Analysis tool and mirrored the result.

FEA and redesign

The load case was a fixed base with 3 tons-force (6,613.86 lbf) applied at the 1 in through hole. The milled part was 6061-T6 aluminum and the cast part grey cast iron. Both original versions exceeded the 275 MPa yield limit at the inner arc.

I removed the rear spine, made the internal wall 0.250 in thick with a 0.500 in offset, tilted the vertical body to 85° from the base, and increased the arc radii (outer to 3.500 in, inner to 1.500 in). On the cast version I also widened the trunk from 2.000 in to 2.500 in.

DESIGN ITERATIONS (YIELD STRENGTH 275 MPA IN THE STUDY)
IterationMaterialWeight (lb)Max stress (MPa)Min. safety factorResult
P1 milledAl 60612.693100.887Failed
P2 castGrey cast iron6.563540.777Failed
P3 milledAl 60612.392860.962Slightly over yield
P4 castGrey cast iron6.532661.033Passed

Safety factor is yield strength divided by maximum stress. P3 is 11 MPa over yield, so I count it as close but not passing.

The milled version got 11% lighter and its peak stress dropped from 310 to 286 MPa. Removing the spine gave a more continuous load path, and the larger radius spreads the bending load across the curve. On the cast version, widening the trunk did most of the work, and the weight barely changed because the spine was gone.

Drawings, assemblies and CAM

  • Drawings: four dimensioned drawings (isometric, top, front, right, section and a detail view) with GD&T for position, perpendicularity, diameter, flatness and symmetry. I wrote up why GD&T tolerances override the title-block tolerances: the title block sets general defaults, while GD&T controls specific features where precision matters.
  • Assembly: press body with pinion, rack, hand wheel and plate, using standard mates, a distance mate on the rack and a rack-and-pinion mate (pitch diameter 0.834 in). I also built a mold assembly from the P2 configuration with a 7.75 × 8.75 × 2.00 in block and the Cavity feature.
  • Mastercam: for the milled part and the mold, OptiRough with a 0.500 in bull nose end mill, then Equal Scallop with a 0.250 in ball nose (stepover around 0.003 in), and a 1.000 in drill for the top hole on the milled part. On the mold I left the through holes out of this stage, since they are better drilled through both halves once assembled.
  • Extra credit: a core-cavity assembly from a shelled P2 configuration, plus programming of the positive mold.
What I'd revisit

The P4 study reports a maximum stress of 266 MPa, but the plot shows no orange or red at that value. I put it down to computational error and did not check further. A mesh refinement would settle it. The rack-and-pinion mate moved the rack as expected, but I saw a misalignment that I left unresolved.

SheetM-2
CourseINTM 439 Advanced Manufacturing, midterm, spring 2026
ToolsSolidWorks, FEA, Mastercam, DMU-50
TaskGo from a scaled DXF to a finished part: model and blueprint, choose the material by FEA, choose stock, plan two machining operations, write a standard operating procedure and quote 50 and 100 parts.

Ye Ole Pop Topper: a bottle opener from DXF to job quote

Result in one lineAluminum 6061-T6 chosen by FEA (safety factor 2 at 50 lbf). Quoted at $1,389.34 for 50 parts and $2,281.40 for 100, about 13 minutes of 5-axis time per part.

Material selection

Removing a cap takes about 25 lbf, so I set the requirement at 50 lbf without yielding, a safety factor above 1 under repeated use, and reasonable cost. I ran a static study for four materials at 50 lbf, then scaled the load up until stress reached yield to estimate a failure force.

FEA RESULTS AT THE 50 LBF TARGET
MaterialSafety factor at 50 lbfEstimated failure load
Aluminum 6061-T62100 lbf
Cast aluminum 356-T61.155.3 lbf
Titanium Ti-6Al-4V6300.3 lbf
AcrylicBelow 115.8 lbf

Acrylic failed outright. Cast aluminum passed, but fails at 55 lbf, which leaves almost no margin for defects and fatigue. Titanium is strong enough but costs roughly 4 to 10 times as much as 6061. I chose 6061-T6.

Stock, workholding and machining

The finished part fits in a 2.5625 × 0.5625 × 0.4375 in block. With machining allowances the minimum stock is 2.6875 × 0.6875 × 0.6875 in, so I chose 0.75 in square 6061 bar, which suppliers commonly stock. Cutting a 2.6875 in blank plus the saw kerf and margin uses 3 in of bar, giving 24 parts from a 6 ft bar. For 50 and 100 parts, 6 ft bars beat 3 ft bars on cost, even with leftover material: $100.59 for three bars (50 parts) and $167.65 for five bars (100 parts) from the cheapest supplier.

The first operation removes most of the material with hard steel jaws. The bar has large parallel faces to clamp and any marks from the jaws are machined off in the second operation. Once the front is shaped there are no flat faces left to clamp, so the second operation uses custom soft jaws machined from aluminum. I chose aluminum over steel (harder, slower to cut, could mark the part) and over 3D-printed jaws (they can wear, compress or warp over 50–100 parts).

  • Operation 1: face mill, contour rough with a 0.3125 in flat end mill, contour finish with a 0.250 in flat end mill, drill the 0.213 in hole, chamfer the edges and the hole. About 7 minutes.
  • Operation 2: soft jaws, face to final thickness, chamfer the back edges and hole. About 3 minutes.
  • Standard operating procedure: an 18-step flow from customer specification through design, stock inspection, soft jaw inspection, both operations and CMM inspection to distribution, with rejection loops at each inspection.
JOB QUOTE
50 parts100 parts
Design and programming (one time)$445.00$445.00
Soft jaw machining (0.25 h)$18.75$18.75
5-axis machining, 13 min per part$825.00$1,650.00
Raw material$100.59$167.65
Total$1,389.34$2,281.40

Roughly $27.79 per part at 50 and $22.81 at 100, as the fixed engineering cost spreads out. Rates: CAD $50/h, programming $65/h, 5-axis $75/h.

What I'd revisit

I would try soft jaws that hold several parts at once to raise throughput. The SOP is drawn as a sequence, but in practice soft jaw machining can overlap with stock inspection and CAM programming can start while procurement is being finalized.

SheetM-3
CourseINTM 439 Advanced Manufacturing, spring 2026
FormatPresentation
ToolsSolidWorks (lofted blade, static FEA), Mastercam 5-axis toolpaths

Two-blade drone propeller: material and machining plan

Result in one lineAluminum 6061-T6 recommended: safety factor 2.62 and 1.07% tip displacement, against a limit of 2%. Nylon and acrylic fail the requirements; titanium passes but costs more to buy and machine.

I modelled the blade by lofting spline-sketched airfoils on four offset planes, where chord, thickness and angle of attack change along the span. Then I added a tip fillet, patterned the blade 180° for the second one, extruded the hub, filleted the hub and blade roots, and cut the center hole.

FEA and material choice

The study fixed the inner hub walls and applied centrifugal load at 10,000 rpm plus a pressure distribution on the lower blade surface, P = 200(r/R)√(1−(r/R)²) with R = 2 in. That pressure is an analytical distribution, not a CFD result, so the ranking of the materials is more reliable than the absolute numbers. I set two requirements: safety factor of at least 1.5, and tip displacement of at most 2% of the blade length.

RESULTS FOR FOUR MATERIALS
MaterialMax stress (MPa)Yield (MPa)Safety factorTip disp. (mm)% of blade lengthResult
Titanium1018278.190.350.68%Pass
Aluminum1052752.620.5461.07%Pass
Nylon93.91391.483.917.70%Fail
Acrylic75.8450.598.5216.77%Fail

Nylon misses the stress requirement narrowly (1.48 against 1.5), but its tip deflection is almost four times the limit. Titanium is strongest, but adds cost and machining difficulty, so I recommended aluminum 6061-T6.

Machining plan

The blade needs 5-axis machining because it twists continuously, and the variable-radius fillet between the round hub and the twisted root cannot be reached by 3-axis tools without collision.

  • Stock and workholding: 4.25 × 1.00 × 0.50 in aluminum bar in a hard-jaw vise with parallels, leaving a floor of stock for jaw support.
  • Operation 1: face with a 2 in face mill, dynamic mill with a 0.625 in end mill, 5-axis OptiRough with a 0.250 in bull end mill, 5-axis Equal Scallop finish with a 0.125 in bull end mill, then drill the 0.125 in center hole.
  • Operation 2: flip the part and hold it on an expanding mandrel through the center hole, then repeat the same toolpath sequence on the second side.

SheetM-4
CourseINTM 439 Advanced Manufacturing, final report, spring 2026
ToolsSolidWorks, Mastercam 5-axis, DMU-50, 3D printing
TaskModel 3-spoke and 4-spoke spinners from a supplied blank, design the workholding, program a four-operation machining process, and quote 50 and 100 parts.

Fidget spinner: CAD, custom workholding and a five-axis job quote

Result in one lineOne workholding scheme (center hole plus one indexed hole) serves both 3- and 4-spoke designs. Quoted at $2,530.75 for 50 parts and $4,320.75 for 100.

Design

The blank is the parent part and each spoke design is a child, so a change to the blank's diameter or height updates both spinners, while edits to one spinner do not touch the parent. To cut the spokes I sketched half of the arc between two spokes (60° for three spokes, 45° for four) and mirrored and patterned it. The 30° outer chamfer is not a standard 45° chamfer tool job, so it is a 5-axis swarf toolpath. The ball-mill edge break is a swept cut, which lets me shift the tool offset so the ball is not fully engaged at its tip.

Stock

The part fits a 2.875 in diameter by 0.28125 in cylinder, so with allowances I chose 3 in diameter 6061-T6 round rod. Each blank uses 0.71875 in of rod, which gives 50 parts from a 3 ft rod and 100 from a 6 ft rod. A 3 ft rod from McMaster-Carr ($202.06) is best for 50 parts. For 100, a 6 ft rod at about $367 from McMaster-Carr or Grainger is cheaper per part. A 12 ft rod was either unavailable or far more expensive per part.

Machining in two phases

Phase 1: blanks. Custom soft jaws hold the round stock, because hard jaws cannot match a circle and tend to mark it. The two operations cut the stock to height, machine the center hole and drill one spoke hole. Those two holes are the locating features for the next phase.

Phase 2: spinner. A custom soft riser with a stepped boss, and a dowel pin in the spoke locating hole, holds the blank in the correct angle. A clamped riser under it lifts the part for spindle clearance during 5-axis moves. Because the datum strategy is a center hole plus one indexed feature, the same workholding works for 3 or 4 spokes.

  • Front operation: face, 2D dynamic mill and contour finish, 30° swarf chamfer, drill and circle-mill the spoke holes, then flowline fillet toolpaths (0.375 in and 0.125 in ball mills) for the countersinks.
  • 4-spoke change: the concave radius between spokes drops from 0.750 in to 0.283 in, which is smaller than the 0.3125 in radius of the 0.625 in end mill. The contour finish needs a 0.3125 in end mill for the 4-spoke design.
  • Back operation: the counterbore side is larger than the riser's step, so a centering sleeve adapts the riser and stops the part moving during machining.
  • Assembly: a bearing is press-fitted in the center with an arbor press, then the 3D-printed thumb piece goes in.

Additive and subtractive together

Soft jaws are machined aluminum because 3D-printed jaws would not resist the cutting forces or hold the datum accuracy across four operations. The centering sleeve and the thumb piece are printed: cheap and quick to change. At larger volumes I would machine the sleeve too, since a printed one would wear and hurt repeatability.

Compared with an impeller

I also compared the process with an impeller job that reuses the same soft jaws and clamped riser. Both start from a parent blank, use the center hole as the primary datum and remove bulk material first. The spinner has one 5-axis toolpath (the chamfer) on a nearly planar part, so it is short. An impeller's twisted blades and small pockets need true 5-axis motion, collision care and conservative feed rates, so the cycle time is much longer.

JOB QUOTE
50 parts100 parts
CAD (models, blueprints, workholding), 7 h$350.00$350.00
Programming (models, workholding), 4 h$260.00$260.00
Workholding machining (soft jaws, fixture, soft riser), 1.25 h$93.75$93.75
5-axis machining, 26 min per part$1,625.00$3,250.00
Raw material (one 3 ft rod, one 6 ft rod)$202.00$367.00
Total$2,530.75$4,320.75

About $50.62 per part at 50 and $43.21 at 100. The 100-part total uses the full $367 for the 6 ft rod; my submitted report used $183.50 in that column by mistake, which gave $4,137.25. The 26 minutes are blank 7 + 3, spinner 8 + 3, and 5 for loading and changing workholding.

What I'd revisit

In Phase 1 a 3-jaw chuck would center the round stock more consistently than soft jaws, because it references the spindle axis directly, while soft jaws have to be machined first and add their own setup error to the tolerance stack-up. I would also machine the centering sleeve instead of printing it if I were running the full quantity.
